title: George Lewis preference and the first public playing at Forester's Hall
summary: Bull and friends prefer George Lewis to white bands, then are pushed into a group at the Forester's Hall jam sessions, playing his only two tunes.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: But, uh, getting back to, uh, the background, um, I wanted to make a point of, uh, of this for a particular reason. It'll come out later. At this stage of the game, this is getting back to our small group in Coogee and Bondi, that's where Jeff Holden left. Um, we started to play and we listened to records and we listened to these George Lewis records, uh, which came out. And we just sort of took them as, as also being jazz records, obviously. But, uh, there was definitely a difference to the sound in those and the sound of the, uh, of the early reissue records. I remember when, when we first bought Jazz at Vespers, we used to play it over and over again, over and over again, Jazz at Vespers. It was a very little time, I think, that, uh, it was a very short time when I, when I ever listened much, with much interest, or, or with much admiration to the early white bands. Especially the Rett Nichols and that sort of business. I mean, uh, I think it's, uh, it's, well, it was to me pretty obvious straight away that there was not much depth in that. And, uh, anyway, we started to, uh, we kept on playing and fiddling around. And we went to the Jazz Club one week, and we used to be there so often that, uh, they sort of got to know us. And they said, well, uh, and they had this, every second Friday night, they used to hire a little, a little old Ramshackle Hall, which, uh, uh, which would really fit well in New Orleans, I've always imagined. It was a Forester's Lodge Hall, and they used to get that, I think, for 10 shillings on, on, on every second Friday night. And all the musicians, um, the jazz musicians in Sydney, when I say all, there was a sort of a clique of them. There were two bands that played at the Sydney Jazz Club, plus other various musicians, used to come along to this hall and just have a, uh, a jam session, and then, and play a few numbers and drink a few bottles and things like this. And, uh, I had a, uh, at that stage of the game, I'd, I'd got rid of my gold trumpet. I realised then that the only thing to do was to play a little, lull, battered cornet. Or I thought, anyway, I don't know, I had a cornet, which was a horrible, atrocious instrument, you know. But it looked good, I thought. Stuck up to play with this group. And I sort of said, boy, no. At that stage of the game, I only knew two tunes. I knew, uh, I'll record cross because I'd listened to the George record so often and learnt the tune. And I knew the first half of Down by the Riverside.
